utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is Case number IT-99-36-R77, contempt proceedings against Maglov.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, everybody. Good afternoon, to you, Ms. Hollis. Good afternoon to you, Ms. Maglov. Let's start with the usual protocol. Ms. Maglov, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand? THE RESPONDENT: Yes, I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Appearances.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: May it please the Court, I am Brenda J. Hollis, and I appear as amicus curiae Prosecutor in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am, and good afternoon to you. Ms. Maglov, I understand that you are representing yourself? THE RESPONDENT: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come to that at a later stage and at the appropriate stage. For the record, I also notice the presence in the courtroom of Madam Korner, Prosecutor in the Brdjanin case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I say, just so it's clear, I'm only here as an observer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And I was going to precisely state that myself with reference to the scheduling order relative to these proceedings. The Trial Chamber had invited both the Prosecution and the Defence to be present if they so wished, having observer status acknowledged in these proceedings. We are going to proceed immediately with the Initial Appearance of respondent Ms. Maglov pursuant to Rule 62 of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Before we do so, however, I would ask Madam Registrar to read out in English Articles 20 and 21 of the Statute as this is a pretty standard procedure in all initial appearances.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Article 20: Commencement and conduct of trial proceedings. The Trial Chamber shall ensure that a trial is fair and expeditious, and the proceedings are conducted in accordance with the rules of procedure and evidence, with full respect for the rights of the accused and due regard for the protection of victims and witnesses. A person against whom an indictment has been confirmed shall, pursuant to an order or an arrest warrant of the International Tribunal, be taken into custody, immediately informed of the charges against him, and transferred to the International Tribunal. The Trial Chamber shall read the indictment, satisfy itself that the rights of the accused are respected, confirm that the accused understands the indictment and instruct the accused to enter a plea. The Trial Chamber shall set a day for trial. The hearings should be public unless the Trial Chamber decides to close the proceedings in accordance with its rules of procedure and evidence. Article 21, rights of the accused. All persons shall be equal before the International Tribunal. In the determination of charges against him, the accused shall be entitled to a fair and public hearing subject to Article 22 of the Statute. The accused shall be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to the provisions of the present Statute. In the determination of any charge against the accused pursuant to the present Statute, the accused shall be entitled to the following minimum guarantees in full equality: (A) to be informed properly and in detail in a language which he understands of the nature and cause of the charge against him; (B) to have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of his defence and to communicate with counsel of his own choosing; (C) to be tried without undue delay; (D) to be tried in his presence, and to defend himself in person or through legal assistance of his own choosing; to be informed, if he does not have legal assistance, of this right; and to have legal assistance assigned to him in any case where the interests of justice so require, and without payment by him in any such case if he does not have sufficient means to pay for it; (E) to examine, or have examined, the witnesses against him and to obtain the attendance and examinations of witnesses on his behalf under the same conditions as witnesses against him; (F) to have the free assistance of an interpreter if he cannot understand or speak the language used in the International Tribunal. (G) not to be compelled to testify against himself or to confess guilt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Registrar. And to that, allow me to add also Rule 45(A) of our Rules of evidence and procedure which strictly speaking is an adjunct to the last paragraph that has been -- paragraph D from Article 21 which has just been read out by Madam Registrar dealing with representation and legal assistance. And Rule 45(A) specifically provides that whenever the interests of justice so demand, counsel shall be assigned to suspects or accused who lack the means to remunerate such counsel. Such assignments shall be treated in accordance with the procedure established in a directive set out by the Registrar and approved by the permanent Judges. Mentioning all this and Article 21(D) has already been read out to you well knowing, we are fully aware that actually this matter has already been dealt with between you and the Registrar of this Tribunal. And that it seems that you have come to the conclusion that -- to represent yourself, to defend yourself in these proceedings. Am I correct? THE RESPONDENT: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that goes on record. And that prompts me to confirm two things: First, that this is a right that you have to defend yourself which you can actually choose and which you have been obviously chosen. At any time you can also decide to be represented at any stage of the proceeding. And that will be dealt in accordance with the Rules. If you do opt to have -- to be represented by another lawyer here, then obviously you are aware that the choice that pertains to you is a choice limited by our Rules. It doesn't mean to say that any lawyer that you would like or you choose to represent you automatically has a right of audience before this Tribunal. There are the Rules and he has to be accepted by the Registrar before he can represent. THE RESPONDENT: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So let's move. Now, Ms. Maglov in particular, and also Ms. Hollis, pursuant to Rule 77(D)(ii) which specifically deals with contempt proceedings, this Trial Chamber, we issued two orders in lieu of an indictment which specify the charges against you. The first of these was issued on the 15th of April 2003, and that is going to be referred to as an order concerning allegations against Milka Maglov. And that order was followed by a scheduling order concerning allegations against Milka Maglov filed on the 18th of November of this year. I want to make sure, first and foremost, Ms. Maglov, that you have been served with both these orders in a language that you understand. THE RESPONDENT: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. But I must add that I was served these papers very late. And this whole procedure of my coming here is really unspeakable. Just to tell you that yesterday, I called the miss from the Registrar's office around 5.00 in the afternoon to tell her that I didn't get my visa, and we were on the hot telephone line. Finally I got my visa, and among other things the airport in Banja Luka was closed due to fog. So I had to travel by bus for eight hours. So basically, due to some technical reasons of my being dislocated here, it is not easy to communicate with Banja Luka. I would kindly ask if possible that I be allocated enough time because practically, the whole procedure started on the 21st of November. And it's the 4th of December today, especially once you have a procedure in motion, I cannot understand why I was issued a visa for two days only, and I have on top of that to travel for 400 kilometres to get a visa, which is a single-entry visa at that. So if anything can be changed concerning all these technicalities, I would be grateful. Also, concerning the orders -- basically, the decisions that I received from the Chambers, I was served, I received them, I understood them. What I'm being charged with, although I did not have an opportunity to see any facts contained in that order. And therefore I find it difficult to state my stance. Your Honours, you know that in this Chamber, when this issue was raised for the first time, I entered a plea, and I still maintain the statement that I made at that time, which is essentially that nothing has changed in the interim period as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Please. I just wanted to confirm for the time being that you have received these orders, which you have confirmed, and you have also confirmed, inter alia, that you have read them and understood their contents. I would expect you to, you being a lawyer yourself. Do you wish these two orders to be read out to you? And the reason why I am putting the question is that these two orders together, as I stated earlier, are in lieu of an indictment. In other words, the accusation, the formality of the accusation against you lies in these two orders. Do you want me or the registrar to read out these two orders in full or not? Or do you exempt -- or do you prefer not to have them read? THE RESPONDENT: [Interpretation] I don't think it's necessary for them to be read out now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Just for the record, however, and also to make things clear, referring to in particular the latter of the two orders, namely, that of the 18th of November 2003, there are two charges that are being brought against you, two counts. One is alleged intimidation of a witness, and the other one, the alleged disclosure of the identity of a witness, of the witness to a member of the public in violation of an order of the Chamber. These are the two charges. My duty is to ask you whether you would like to enter a plea on either or both of these two charges today. THE RESPONDENT: [Interpretation] You want me to enter a plea concerning my guilt, what I think about these two accusations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's make it clear. You have an option if you want to tell me, "Judge, I would like to think about it. According to the Rules, I have a time limit of 30 days, which I can even shorten. And then I will enter the plea after that time limit has passed." However, that would mean you will have to come back again for the simple purpose of entering a plea. It's up to you. I mean -- you also have the choice of entering the plea today which will be a very simple plea of either not guilty or guilty. Nothing else in addition to that for the time being. THE RESPONDENT: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. My intention is to enter a plea. I don't think that I'm guilty of anything. Furthermore, I don't think that I did anything wrongly, even without intention, and that I hindered the work of this Tribunal in any manner whatsoever. I have been a lawyer for 30 years now, and my whole life I saw myself as a servant of a court who was there to help the court, not to hinder its work. So therefore, I don't feel guilty on any count.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So for the record, please, Madam Registrar, enter that Ms. Maglov entered a -- pleaded not guilty to both counts. Ms. Maglov, it is also my duty to inform you and advise you that pursuant to Rule 62 bis, the fact that you have entered a plea of not guilty today does not preclude you from changing your plea in due course. You are also free to contact the Prosecutor, Ms. Hollis, in this case, should you like to initiate discussions with her along the lines or in the direction of a possible change of plea or anything along those lines anyway. We are going to convert ourselves now into a Status Conference straight away in order to speed up proceedings, because the alternative would be to stop here, and then convene a Status Conference, and ask you to come back again, and ask Ms. Hollis to come back again. These being contempt proceedings, we thought it fit, provided there are no objections coming from either of you, to hold a Status Conference today, too, to thrash out the business that is actually reserved to the status conferences that are held in other big cases, not like this one. Rule 77(E) of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence in fact, stipulates that parts 4 to 8 of the Rules shall apply mutatis mutandis to contempt proceedings and on the basis of that Rule, on that provision of our Rules, we are now going to deal, as stated, with some of the issues that are normally on the agenda of any Status Conference held by this Tribunal. You are all aware that Rule 65 bis basically envisages as the purpose of Status Conferences to organise exchanges between the parties so as to ensure an expeditious preparation for the trial, and also to give an opportunity to you, in this case, Ms. Maglov, to raise any issue in relation to your mental or physical condition, which in this case, I suppose, you not being in detention does not really come into question. But however, it's still there, and you can raise any such matter if it is the case. My -- our legal staff have informed us that both you, Ms. Hollis, and you, Ms. Maglov, have given an indication that it is your desire to conduct further investigations before this trial really commences, before the hearing of the evidence. We come to the stage of the hearing of the evidence. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution has requested that the Registry provide an investigator to conduct certain additional investigation in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Ms. Maglov? THE RESPONDENT: [Interpretation] I have no proposal in that direction concerning investigations. I believe that there are statements of all parties concerned, and there is a limited number of witnesses that can have anything to say about this topic. There are in total four people who are able to say something about this case. But if the Prosecution thinks so, then it's okay with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I will not stop either you or the Prosecution in case you want time to conduct further investigations. This is a right that you have, and I will allow you what we consider to be enough space for this purpose. Feel free to conduct your own investigations if you so desire. THE RESPONDENT: [Interpretation] I don't wish to conduct any investigation whatsoever. There's no reason for that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Hollis, you will understand also that this Trial Chamber is not in a position to give you all the time that you would wish to conduct and conclude these investigations. There is a time limit that we will be suggesting, which we hope you will accept. If you don't accept it, then obviously we have to think about what to do. Have you got an idea as to how much time you require for these investigations?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As I indicated, I have submitted a letter to the Registry requesting that an investigator be appointed. It would appear logical to use the investigator who did the amicus investigation since he is already familiar with the case. I have spoken with that individual, and he has indicated that he would be available. It would be my intention, depending upon when this person was appointed, to have a meeting with this person before the end of December to set out exactly what it is that I would like pursued, and he has indicated he's available in January to pursue that. It is not a great deal of additional investigation that I have in mind. It is follow-up investigation with three persons who have already been spoken with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: -- and initial investigation or initial interviews with two additional people with a possibility of two others depending upon how inquiries would progress.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And I anticipate, Your Honour, it would be approximately 18 hours for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Disclosure matters, you're both familiar with the procedure. Ms. Maglov because she has been counsel here, and Ms. Hollis also because you have been a member of the Office of the Prosecutor in the past. There are two kinds of disclosure -- three kinds, actually, that I would like to deal with. First is disclosure under Rule 66. That is disclosure by the Prosecutor. I take it that the material supporting the order, our decision in lieu of the indictment, has already been disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I wasn't privy to those proceedings, and I'm not quite sure what was relied upon. To the extent the report of the amicus was relied upon, it's my understanding that Ms. Maglov already has that report. If additional materials were relied upon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, there's no additional material that was relied upon. It's just the statements that were made here in -- during the trial in Brdjanin, including also statements made by Ms. Maglov herself and statements made by Mr. Ackerman and statements made by Ms. Korner. And then, of course, the records of the findings and report of the previous amicus curiae. Those you are in possession of already, Ms. Maglov, I take it? THE RESPONDENT: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, it's almost time. Okay. It's almost needless to point out, Ms. Hollis, that should you conduct further investigations and these be redacted in writing. Copies must be handed over, disclosed, to Ms. Maglov. I'm going to mention the deadline now, this being actually a deadline to which I will be referring later on, and that will be not later than the 19th of January of 2004. By that date, copies of any such statements need to be -- or other evidence, be it documentary or whatever, needs to be disclosed to Ms. Maglov. Then, in case there is any, you also have a responsibility under Rule 68 to disclose exculpatory material. And I draw your attention, both of you, to Rule 67, which deals with reciprocal disclosure, should that arise at any particular point in time later on. Rule 65 ter (F) requires the Prosecutor - in this case, you, Ms. Hollis - to file a pre-trial brief. And Rule 65 ter (G) also requires you, Ms. Maglov, to file a Defence brief. Given the relative simplicity of these proceedings, I am going to set deadlines to both of you for the filing of these briefs. The idea is to lay the ground, make it possible for this case to be heard and disposed with as quickly as possible, without the need of you having to come here again and again and again, which I understand can become quite costly and quite an inconvenience. So I would ask both of you to cooperate with the Trial Chamber in the effort that it is making to streamline the proceedings and to simplify them as much as possible. The Prosecution will have until the 19th of January 2004 to file its pre-trial brief, and the Defence will have until the 9th of February to file its brief. The Trial Chamber will change any or either of or both these two deadlines only if there is justification. Otherwise, these two deadlines will stay. It is the intention of this Trial Chamber to set the date of the trial for the week in February starting on the 16th. Our opinion as at present, but subject to going through any further documentation that we might have later on, we might receive from you, is that we anticipate the case for the Defence and -- the case for the Prosecution and the case for the Defence to be concluded in two days; 16th and 17th. I think that is perfectly possible. However, we will be at your disposal that week should the need arise for more time. I think we can anticipate you should be in a position to conclude in two days. Please try to make an effort. If there are problems you have, you are free to discuss amongst yourselves and come back with any concrete proposals to the Trial Chamber. We are open to consider any other suggestion which you might have should it not be convenient or practically possible for you to finish your case in the two days I indicated. I will be blocking the entire week for the case should the need for the entire week be there. But otherwise, please try to finish in less than the five days that I have mentioned. As of now, do you have any problems with the trial taking place in the week starting on the 16th of February, 2004?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you, Ms. Maglov? THE RESPONDENT: [Interpretation] The only thing I don't know is that concerning weather conditions because in our country in February, snow could be very strong and high. Probably the airports could be closed and other technical problems. But as far as I'm personally concerned, it's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. If there are such problems, you will find that the Trial Chamber will fully understand the situation, and that's not something that you should bother about. Do any of you wish to raise any other matter? Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I would raise two matters. The first matter concerns what version of Rule 77 will be applied to these proceedings. From reviewing the materials that I received, it appears to me that the relevant time period for the alleged misconduct was from about the beginning of September until about the end of December 2001. And when I look at the version of Rule 77 which was in effect at that time, it was -- based on a compilation of the Rules that has been provided to me, it was the Rule from the 23rd Plenary Session, 1 and 13 December 2000. And under part A of that Rule as it read then, it indicated that any person who, and then listed subcategories. Of course, as we know, the Rule then was changed so that today, and in fact, as of the 25th Plenary Session, the Rule begins in part A: "The Tribunal in the exercise of its inherent power may hold in contempt those who knowingly and willfully interfere with the administration of justice including ..." So that the language "knowing" and "knowingly and willfully" was not part of the Rule in part A in September of 2001. Certainly the change in the language, I believe, ensures to the benefit of the accused, and for that reason you may wish to apply this latter Rule. But it would be helpful to know with certainty which Rule you would apply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis, I'm going to disappoint you. There is no way I'm going to be helpful because this, I anticipate, will be one of the submissions. What you can legally take for granted is that when we handed down our decision, our order of March 2003, we could have only been applying at the time Rule 77 as it was then.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, there is a Rule which is dated -- an order which is dated 18th of November. This is basically a scheduling order. If we are talking of substantive law, then I don't think I should say much. And if we are talking of procedural law, you are fully aware of what the Rule in criminal law, procedural law is when there is a change in the procedure in the course of the proceedings. I will not, of course, say more than that because this could be the subject matter of submissions that will be made either by you but probably even more by Ms. Maglov herself. We, therefore, have to reserve our position. But we cannot decide the matter. Even if you are raising the matter now, we are fully aware of it. We were fully aware of it when we took part in the Plenary Session that changed the Rule itself. But in any case, these are matters which -- these are your problems at the moment and Ms. Maglov's problems, and they will be our problem later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I'm happy to deal with it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Rules are common Rules applied in substantive criminal law and in procedural law. And I suppose you're both aware of them, and we will not depart from those Rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. The second matter, Your Honour, has to do with a potential witness who may be called in these proceedings. And that potential is the lead Defence counsel in the Brdjanin case. And I raise this to put -- simply to advise the Court that the Prosecution may call this person because it may have an impact on the appropriate constitution of the panel that hears this contempt proceeding. So I wanted to advise you of that possibility so that Your Honours could take that into consideration in determining if that should warrant a change of the composition of the Chamber that hears this contempt proceeding. And that's the reason that I raise that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are fully aware of that. Not that you are going to mention, but about the possibility of Mr. Ackerman being summoned as a witness in these proceedings. I suppose that he, too, is aware of that possibility. He hinted at that at some point in time months ago. And that's why, rightly so, he wanted to keep away from the matter and from the proceedings itself. It's up to you. We'll come to that if and when. We may be in full disagreement on whether that should have an effect or impact on the composition of this Trial Chamber. Anyway ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: As I said, Your Honour, I simply wanted to advise you that that was a possibility so you could consider the potential implications of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And that's all I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Maglov, is there any matter you would like to raise? THE RESPONDENT: [Interpretation] First of all, there's another technical issue, or rather an error in these decisions. I have not referred to this before. It states that I had been a Defence counsel since September, which is not correct. It was only as of November. There's another question I have. Is it possible perhaps for the Registrar to copy today's transcript on to a floppy disk for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure that is possible, Ms. Maglov. I'm pretty sure that is. And Madam Registrar, could you take care of that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No problem, as always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. THE RESPONDENT: [Interpretation] In view of this fact that I had only been Defence counsel as of November and not as of September, I believe that as for the second part, on both counts, Mr. Ackerman will prove a key witness in this case. Just a remark I wish to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. In other words, if you don't call him, she will call him. All right, but I am also bound by the Rules to ask you if there is any matter related to your health that you would like to raise? I suppose not. As it might relate to these proceedings. THE RESPONDENT: [Interpretation] I'm sorry I have to say this, but these whole proceedings have caused me a great deal of stress. Since the whole thing started, I have suffered high blood pressure, and I am undergoing constant therapy. It is no pleasant thing, I can assure you, especially when one knows that one has done nothing wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will take that into consideration as well, Ms. Maglov. That should bring our proceedings to an end today. So the parties are put on notice that with or without further investigations being conducted by either or both of them, we'll have a pre-trial brief by 19 January, Defence brief by 9 February. And please God, hopefully we should start on the 16th of February and try to finish as early as possible. THE RESPONDENT: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I've understood that. The only thing I have not understood is whether I'll be receiving this pre-trial brief also by the 19th of February. That is prior to filing my own pre-trial brief. That's the only thing I wanted to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Hollis, in this case, there is the abnormal situation of the respondent not being resident here in The Hague where she can be served with a copy of your brief practically the same day or the day after. So if you could possibly keep that in mind and try to have a copy served on Ms. Maglov, even unofficially, an unofficial copy serve on her -- do you have a fax?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We have been serving her all the documents by fax or email from Registry. As soon as we receive a filing, we send a fax to her residence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long does that take?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long does it take to fax the documents to Ms. Maglov after the document has been filed? One day, two days, three days? What?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Same day, basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then it shouldn't be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, also we have the point, not only does Ms. Maglov not reside here, neither do I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, we know.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So that I will be couriering to the Tribunal my pre-trial brief, and I will have to request the assistance of the Registry to determine the most expeditious means to actually send the information to Ms. Maglov, the disclosure information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Maglov, you have, I suppose, given Ms. Hollis your telephone numbers, where you can be reached in other words? THE RESPONDENT: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate that. We can call it a day. We stand adjourned. And the next time we meet, the trial should start. All right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: at 5.02 p.m.
